chapter.title: Work orders in small pieces: one feature at a time

cards.body:
You ask a builder for a new kitchen, a new bathroom and a new roof, all by Friday. On Saturday the hallway floods. Which of the three jobs did it?

Good contractors avoid that riddle with **work orders**: one job, inspect it, sign it off, then start the next. You can hand Claude Code the same kind of slip.
cards.simpler: Picture asking a builder for a new kitchen, a new bathroom and a new roof, all done by Friday. On Saturday the hallway floods. Which job caused it? Good builders avoid that puzzle with **work orders**. They do one job, check it, sign it off, and only then start the next one. You can give Claude Code the same kind of slip.

cards.prompt: Maya sends Claude one message asking for five new things in her habit tracker. Afterwards, the tick button that worked yesterday does nothing. What's her real problem now?

options.text: Claude skipped part of the request because five things is too many.
She can't tell which of the five changes broke the button.
The app is now too big for her computer to run.

whyNot.a: That's a limit Claude doesn't really have. It will happily try all five, and the trouble starts after it does.
whyNot.c: That's worrying about size, but size isn't the issue. Five small features barely make the app bigger. What changed is how many places a fault could hide.

cards.reteach: When five things change at once and one thing breaks, you have five suspects. When one thing changes, you have one. The asking is never the hard part. Finding the leak afterwards is.

cards.title: One job, one suspect
cards.body:
You'd think asking for five features at once saves time. It does, right up until something breaks. Then you're a plumber in a house where five people worked the same afternoon, tapping every pipe.

**Ask for one job, test it, save it.** That's the whole loop. Testing means using the app the way a person would: click the button, type the thing, refresh the page.

Saving means a Git commit from chapter 5, a save point you can go back to. If job four goes wrong, you step back to the end of job three, not to last Tuesday.
cards.simpler: Asking for five features at once feels faster, until something breaks. Then you're a plumber in a house where five people worked that afternoon, checking every pipe. **Ask for one job, test it, save it.** Testing means using the app like a person would: click the button, type something, reload the page. Saving means a Git commit from chapter 5, a point you can return to. If job four breaks, you go back to the end of job three, not last Tuesday.

cards.title: Maya's habit tracker, take one
cards.body: Maya types one long message: add habits, tick them off each day, a streak counter, dark mode and a weekly chart. Claude edits 9 files in one go. The chart is lovely. It charts nothing. The streak counter is stuck at 0, and dark mode has made the tick button black on black. **Her last save point is from before all five**, so going back means losing the parts that did work.
cards.simpler: Maya sends one long message asking for five things: adding habits, ticking them off each day, a streak counter, dark mode and a weekly chart. Claude changes 9 files at once. The chart looks great but shows nothing. The streak counter stays stuck at 0. Dark mode turned the tick button black on a black background. **Her last save point is from before all five**, so going back means losing the parts that worked.

cards.prompt: Take two. Maya asks only for job 1: 'let me add a habit by typing its name.' She tests it, and 'drink water' shows up, even after a refresh. What now?

options.text: Ask for jobs 2 to 5 together, since job 1 went smoothly.
Save it as a commit, then ask for job 2 on its own.
Ask for job 2 now, and save both jobs together at the end.

whyNot.a: That's take one again, just starting later. Four jobs at once means four suspects when something breaks.
whyNot.c: That skips the save without saving any time. If job 2 breaks something, she has no clean point where job 1 worked on its own.

cards.reteach: Each finished job gets its own save point, the way a builder gets a sign-off before starting the next room. Test, save, then ask again. If the next job goes wrong, you only lose that one job.

cards.title: Splitting the big idea
cards.body:
So how do you turn 'a habit tracker' into small jobs? **A job is the right size when you can test it with a few clicks.** 'Add a streak counter' passes. 'Make it nice' doesn't.

Claude can help you split it. Ask: 'Split this app into 6 small jobs, each one I can test by clicking. Don't build anything yet.' Keep the list in a file, like a numbered work order taped to the fridge.

Order matters. The frame goes up before the paint: main jobs first, dark mode last. *The Pragmatic Programmer*, a classic book for coders, argues for the same rhythm: small steps, each one checked.
cards.simpler: **A job is the right size when you can test it with a few clicks.** 'Add a streak counter' passes. 'Make it nice' doesn't. Claude can do the splitting. Ask: 'Split this app into 6 small jobs, each one I can test by clicking. Don't build anything yet.' Keep the list in a file. Order matters: main jobs first, dark mode last, like walls going up before paint. The classic coding book *The Pragmatic Programmer* agrees: small steps, each one checked.

cards.body: Sam asks for job 3, a reminder message, and it works. Pleased, Sam adds: 'while you're in there, also make the buttons rounder and add a little sound.' That's **three jobs wearing one job's coat**. To catch it in your own messages, look for 'also' or 'while you're at it'. Cut everything after those words and save it for its own turn.
cards.simpler: Sam asks for job 3, a reminder message, and it works. Happy, Sam adds: 'while you're in there, also make the buttons rounder and add a little sound.' That's **three jobs wearing one job's coat**. To spot this in your own messages, watch for the words 'also' or 'while you're at it'. Cut everything after them and save it for its own turn.

cards.prompt: Maya's list has room for one more job. Which one is the right size to hand over?

options.text: Build the rest of the tracker: streaks, charts and reminders.
Add a tick button next to each habit that turns green when clicked.
Make the app feel better and fix anything that looks off.

whyNot.a: That's the whole house, not one work order: three jobs, so three suspects.
whyNot.c: That's 'make it better' from chapter 2. It has no finish line, so no click can tell you it's done.

cards.reteach: A good work order has one job and one way to check it. Ask yourself: what would I click to know this is done? If you can name one click and the result you'd see, it's the right size.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Ask Claude for one job, test it like a user, save it, then ask for the next. **Big ideas become a numbered list of 5 to 8 small jobs, main jobs first and polish last**, each small enough to check in a few clicks.

Tomorrow: the builder forgets everything overnight, unless you leave it a note.
cards.simpler: Ask Claude for one job, test it the way a user would, save it, then ask for the next. **Big ideas become a numbered list of 5 to 8 small jobs, main jobs first and polish last.** Polish means the finishing touches. Each job should be small enough to check with a few clicks. Tomorrow: the builder forgets everything overnight, unless you leave it a note.

cards.body: Open Claude Code in your project folder and type: 'Split my app idea into 6 small jobs I can each test by clicking. Don't build anything yet.' Read the list. Any polish near the top? Move it down.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in your project folder and type: 'Split my app idea into 6 small jobs I can each test by clicking. Don't build anything yet.' Read the list it gives you. Do you see any finishing touches, like dark mode, near the top? **Move the polish down to the end.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now turn an app idea into 5 to 8 small jobs and build them one at a time, with a save point after each.
